plot_extraction.response_text:
Nineteen-year-old Tom Collins, nearly penniless and repeatedly rejected for newspaper work, applies to the city editor of a major Washington paper. The editor initially dismisses the inexperienced youth, but Tom’s spirited demand for a fair chance earns him a nearly impossible test: obtain from Senator August the secret result of a political conference that every experienced reporter has failed to uncover.

Learning that the senator has left by train, Tom races to the station, boards the departing express, and finds him. Senator August refuses to reveal anything, but Tom’s honesty, courtesy, and determination win his sympathy. During the journey, an urgent telegram arrives warning that continued silence about the conference is politically damaging. Forced to release the news immediately, the senator dictates the official statement to Tom before he leaves the train at the next junction.

Tom returns to Washington and delivers the story after the regular edition’s deadline. Because the senator will not issue the statement elsewhere until later, the paper can publish an extra with the year’s biggest exclusive. Impressed by Tom’s resourcefulness and success, the city editor hires him as a reporter, instructing him to report promptly at eight the next morning.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the brisk, optimistic style of an early twentieth-century newspaper-adventure tale. Its prose is clear, accessible, and strongly plot-driven, with an emphasis on professional initiation, personal pluck, and success earned through persistence. The narrative follows a conventional rise-from-desperation arc: an impoverished and inexperienced young man is given an apparently impossible test, pursues it with determination, benefits from a credible turn of fortune, and proves his worth. Suspense comes less from danger than from deadlines, missed connections, limited money, and the uncertainty of whether Tom will secure both the political statement and a position.

The narration is third-person and closely aligned with Tom Collins’s perspective. Although the narrator occasionally steps back to make general observations—such as the reflection on how starvation appears to a healthy nineteen-year-old—the reader usually experiences events through Tom’s anxiety, discouragement, calculation, and growing confidence. Free indirect phrasing conveys his thoughts without sharply separating them from the narration, particularly in passages where he assesses the hopelessness of his assignment. This close focalisation makes the story emotionally immediate while preserving the orderly authority of an omniscient or semi-omniscient storyteller.

The diction is straightforward but carries a distinctly period flavour. Terms such as “city editor,” “copy paper,” “Pullman,” “Associated Press,” “copy-cutter,” and “plate” establish the material culture and working practices of a metropolitan newspaper office. Expressions including “pluck,” “my lad,” “forlorn hope,” “worm out of him,” and “bare fighting chance” reflect the idiom of popular fiction of the era. Descriptions are economical and character-oriented rather than decorative: the editor’s “fierce and bristling mustache,” black pipe, threatening glare, and vindictive pencil strokes immediately turn him into an intimidating comic type. The senator’s gray tweeds, military bearing, and shrewd but kindly face similarly provide a compact visual and moral portrait.

Sentence structure varies according to emotional pressure. Expository sections use balanced, moderately long sentences to explain Tom’s circumstances or the national political stakes, while moments of urgency shift toward shorter clauses, abrupt questions, and rapid action verbs. Repetition and interruption are prominent devices. The opening recurrence of “again” dramatises Tom’s hesitation, and dashes reproduce faltering thought: “Another failure and—what?” or “unless—unless fortune favored him.” Tom’s frequent stammers and self-corrections reveal nervousness, whereas the editor’s clipped questions and commands communicate authority. As Tom gains confidence, his speech becomes firmer and more direct, so changes in syntax function as markers of character development.

Dialogue occupies much of the story and is the principal means of characterisation. The city editor speaks in sarcasm, challenges, and brusque imperatives; his hostility tests applicants and conceals professional judgment rather than simple cruelty. Senator August’s initially laconic answers gradually lengthen and soften as Tom’s honesty interests him. Tom remains respectful but persistent, distinguishing himself from stereotypically aggressive reporters. The exchanges are often lightly comic, especially when Tom admits that he has been a reporter for only half an hour or forgets that he cannot afford the train fare. Dialogue also keeps exposition active: professional standards, political circumstances, and Tom’s background emerge through confrontation rather than static description.

The pacing is carefully accelerated. The hesitant opening delays entry into the office, creating a contrast with the speed that follows. Once Tom receives the assignment, the story becomes a chain of timed movements: the senator has left ten minutes earlier, the train departs at 2.20, Tom has six minutes to catch it, the junction is eight minutes away, and the newspaper’s final edition is due at five. Clock references, transport changes, telegrams, and newsroom procedures produce a mechanical forward momentum appropriate to journalism. A compact political exposition temporarily slows the action but raises the value of the prospective scoop by explaining why the conference matters nationally.

The tone blends earnestness, suspense, humour, and sentiment without becoming heavily melodramatic. Tom’s poverty is treated seriously, yet the narrative avoids prolonged pathos. Comic touches—the enormous shears, the editor writing as though composing an enemy’s death sentence, Tom’s outdated mental image of a senator, and the forgotten train fare—keep the adventure buoyant. The coincidence that delivers the decisive telegram is openly framed as luck, but it does not wholly replace merit: Tom creates the opportunity by pursuing the senator, behaves tactfully enough to win his sympathy, knows shorthand, and works quickly under pressure.

The political background is broad and functional rather than deeply analytical. Conflict over currency reform and sectional divisions within the Democratic Party lend realism and public significance to the assignment, but politics primarily serves as the mechanism for a journalistic “beat.” The story’s deeper interest lies in work, character, and professional competence. It celebrates courage, initiative, punctuality, resourcefulness, and the ability to act despite uncertainty. It also presents the newspaper office as a severe meritocracy whose rituals are intimidating but ultimately fair to anyone who demonstrates useful talent.

Structurally, the story relies on reversal and delayed recognition. Tom first retreats, then confronts the editor; the impossible assignment becomes possible; the senator’s refusal becomes cooperation; the missed regular edition becomes an exclusive extra; and the editor’s apparent dismissal becomes an offer of employment. The final exchange repeats the editor’s habitual severity while changing its meaning. He gives no explicit praise, but the instruction to arrive at eight confirms Tom’s success. The concluding sound of the presses provides an emphatic auditory image, linking Tom’s personal triumph to the machinery of the profession he has entered. Overall, the style is energetic, morally affirmative, lightly humorous, and engineered for a satisfying final payoff.

# A Bare Fighting Chance

Again Tom Collins walked past the entrance of the *Washington Evening Star*.

Again he turned at the corner, came back slowly, and studied the brass letters upon the glass doors as though he had never seen them before.

He had seen them often enough. During the past fortnight he had presented himself at nearly every newspaper office in Washington, and at several of them twice. At each he had received substantially the same answer.

“No vacancy.”

“No experience? Then we can’t use you.”

“Try us again in six months.”

Six months! Tom thrust a hand into his pocket and counted, by touch, the coins there. Twenty-seven cents would scarcely maintain a healthy nineteen-year-old for six months. Indeed, it promised a doubtful dinner and a still more doubtful breakfast. Starvation, when regarded from a comfortable chair, may appear a romantic misfortune; but to a young fellow with broad shoulders and an excellent appetite it is a plain and immediate nuisance.

He stopped once more before the entrance.

Another failure and—what?

There was no answer to that question. His room rent was two days overdue. His landlady had been patient because he reminded her of a son in Ohio, but sons in Ohio did not pay Washington rents. Tom had already sold his watch and the better of his two suits. The suit he wore had been brushed until brushing could do no more for it.

This time he went in.

The elevator carried him to the third floor, where a long passage trembled with the vibration of presses below. Boys hurried through swinging doors. Bells rang. Typewriters clicked in a score of different keys, producing a tremendous and disorderly tune. Somewhere a man shouted for copy, and another man shouted that he had sent it five minutes before.

Tom’s heart quickened. The confusion did not repel him. It seemed to him the most splendidly purposeful confusion in the world.

A copy boy, small, freckled, and immensely important, looked him over.

“Want somebody?”

“The city editor.”

“Got an appointment?”

“No.”

The boy grinned as one who had discovered a dangerous lunatic.

“Name?”

“Thomas Collins.”

“Business?”

“I want work.”

The grin broadened.

“Wait.”

He vanished through a gate in the railing. Beyond it Tom could see rows of desks buried beneath papers, paste pots, telegraph slips, and battered reference books. In the centre sat a large man with a fierce and bristling mustache. A black pipe projected from one corner of his mouth. He was cutting a column from another newspaper with shears large enough, Tom thought, to trim a hedge.

The boy whispered to him. The large man glanced up, and his eyes met Tom’s. It was not an encouraging glance.

“Tell him no,” he said.

Tom heard it distinctly.

The boy returned.

“Mr. Pike says there ain’t anything.”

Tom had expected the answer; nevertheless, it struck him with the force of a door slammed in his face. He thanked the boy, turned, and walked halfway to the elevator.

Then something in him rebelled.

For two weeks he had been civil, humble, and easily dismissed. He had accepted the judgment of clerks who had not read a line he had written and editors who had not permitted him to speak three sentences. He had been told that he lacked experience, as if experience were an article a man might purchase before breakfast.

He turned so suddenly that the copy boy nearly collided with him.

“Mr. Pike!” Tom called.

The typewriters seemed to pause, though in truth they did not. The large man removed his pipe.

“Well?”

“I should like to speak to you myself.”

“You have spoken. What is it?”

“A job.”

“Haven’t one.”

“How do you know you haven’t one for me?”

Mr. Pike laid down his shears. Several reporters nearby became interested without appearing to do so.

“Because,” said the editor, “I know my business.”

“I don’t doubt it, sir. But you don’t know me.”

“No,” returned Mr. Pike, “and at present I’m bearing up wonderfully under the deprivation.”

A reporter coughed into his hand.

Tom’s face grew hot, but he stood his ground.

“I’ve been trying every paper in the city. They all say I have no experience. I can’t get experience unless somebody lets me work. I don’t ask you to hire me because I need the money. I ask you to give me a fair chance to show whether I’m useful.”

Mr. Pike took the pipe from his mouth and regarded him more closely.

“How old?”

“Nineteen.”

“College?”

“One year.”

“Why only one?”

“My father died.”

“Ever written anything?”

“For a weekly paper in Pennsylvania. Farm notices, school meetings, an obituary, and part of a fire.”

“Part of a fire?”

“The press broke down before we printed the rest.”

This time the reporter’s cough sounded suspiciously like a laugh.

Mr. Pike scowled at him, then picked up a blue pencil and drew a vindictive line through half a page of copy.

“Know shorthand?”

“Yes, sir.”

“How fast?”

“One hundred and ten words a minute if the speaker behaves reasonably.”

“Speakers never do. Know the city?”

“Fairly well.”

“Know politics?”

“Enough to learn more.”

“Every young fool knows politics.” Mr. Pike pointed his pencil as if passing sentence. “Do you know Senator August?”

“I know who he is.”

“Have you met him?”

“No, sir.”

“Good. That puts you on the same footing as the rest of mankind. Now listen.”

He leaned back, and the men at neighboring desks ceased even pretending not to hear.

At noon that day there had been a private conference at the Willard Hotel. Senator Jonathan August, senior senator from a Western state and chairman of an important party committee, had met four other leaders to consider the proposed currency bill then dividing their party. Eastern Democrats feared inflation; Western and Southern members demanded an enlargement of the circulating medium; and the Administration, anxious to offend no one, was in a fair way to offend everybody. For three weeks rumors had multiplied. That morning’s conference was expected either to unite the factions or split them beyond repair.

Every newspaper in Washington wanted the result.

Every newspaper had failed to get it.

“The Associated Press man tried,” said Mr. Pike. “The senator told him the weather was pleasant. Jenkins of the *Courier* tried. He got a remark on the condition of Pennsylvania Avenue. Our own man waited two hours and learned that Senator August prefers gray gloves. The conference is over, the politicians are scattered, and nobody will say whether they agreed, quarreled, or threw the currency bill out of a window.”

He bent suddenly toward Tom.

“Get me the result.”

Tom stared at him.

“From Senator August?”

“From Senator August.”

“When?”

“Now.”

“But if experienced men—”

“You wanted a fair chance.”

“Yes, sir, but—”

“Was it a fair chance you wanted, or a comfortable chair?”

Tom straightened.

“Where is the senator?”

Mr. Pike’s mustache moved slightly. Perhaps it concealed a smile; perhaps not.

“He left the Willard ten minutes ago. Find him. Get a statement in his own words. Bring it here before five o’clock. If it is worth printing, I’ll pay you space rates. If it is the truth, and exclusive, I may let you come back tomorrow.”

“Is that an offer of a position?”

“It is an offer of a forlorn hope. Take it or stop blocking the aisle.”

Tom took his hat from beneath his arm.

“I’ll take it.”

“Then why are you standing there?”

Tom ran.

At the Willard he found three discouraged reporters in the lobby and a clerk who had no reason to protect the senator now that he had gone.

“Senator August left for the Union Station,” the clerk said. “He is taking the two-twenty express west.”

Tom looked at the clock.

It was fourteen minutes past two.

The distance to the station was not great for a carriage, but Tom possessed twenty-seven cents, and a carriage driver would not be moved by professional enthusiasm. He dashed into the street, dodged a cable car, and ran.

His hat blew off at the first corner. A colored messenger boy caught it neatly and held it out. Tom snatched it with a breathless “Thanks!” and went on. A stout gentleman stepped from a shop and was obliged to jump back. A policeman shouted something. Tom neither heard nor cared.

Six minutes!

The station clock showed nineteen minutes after two when he burst through the doors. A gate was closing at the end of the concourse.

“Western express?” he gasped.

“Track four. She’s moving.”

Tom raced past the gatekeeper, who made an unsuccessful grab for his sleeve. The long train had begun to glide beneath the iron roof. Porters were lifting the steps. At the rear of the last Pullman, a conductor swung aboard.

“Wait!” Tom cried.

The conductor did not wait. Trains, unlike editors, cannot be argued with.

Tom ran beside the last car. For several seconds it gained on him; then he caught the brass rail, found the lower step with one foot, and swung himself up. The conductor seized his collar and dragged him onto the platform.

“Are you trying to get killed?”

“No, sir,” Tom panted. “I’m trying to become a reporter.”

The conductor looked as though he considered the first ambition more reasonable.

“Ticket?”

Tom put a hand into his pocket.

Then he remembered.

In the excitement of pursuit, he had overlooked the minor fact that railway companies expected passengers to pay. His twenty-seven cents would not carry him far toward the West.

“I—haven’t bought one.”

“Cash fare, then.”

“How far is the next stop?”

“Brenton Junction.”

“What is the fare?”

“Eighty cents.”

Tom’s spirits descended even more rapidly than his breathing.

“I have twenty-seven.”

“Then you’ve got trouble.”

“I must see Senator August. It is a matter of national importance.”

“Of course it is. It generally is when a man hasn’t a ticket.”

“Let me speak to him. If he refuses to see me, put me off at Brenton. I’ll send the fare to the company tonight.”

“You’ll send it from the middle of Maryland, I suppose.”

“I’ll leave my coat.”

The conductor glanced at the coat and evidently concluded that the railway could struggle on without it.

“I’ll leave my shoes,” Tom added.

“What good would that do me?”

“None, sir. But it would prove I mean to pay.”

The conductor’s stern mouth twitched.

“You newspaper fellows are all touched in the head.”

“I’ve only been one for half an hour.”

“That explains why you’re worse than the others.” He jerked his thumb toward the car. “Go on. If the senator throws you out, don’t expect me to slow down.”

Tom entered the Pullman.

Senator August was not difficult to identify, though he did not resemble Tom’s old mental picture of a senator. There was no tall hat, no flowing black coat, no bundle of state papers beneath his arm. He sat beside a window in gray tweeds, reading a magazine. He was erect, broad-chested, and white-haired, with a military mustache and a face at once shrewd and kindly.

Tom paused to recover his breath and arrange his collar. Then he approached.

“Senator August?”

The senator looked up.

“Yes?”

“My name is Thomas Collins. I represent the *Evening Star*.”

This was not exactly false, though Tom felt the phrase wore a coat rather too large for it.

“No interviews,” said the senator, and returned to his magazine.

“I beg your pardon, sir, but I must ask one question.”

“You may ask it. I shall not answer.”

“What was decided at the conference this morning?”

“Nothing for publication.”

“Did the committee agree upon its policy?”

“Nothing for publication.”

“Will you support the currency bill in its present form?”

The senator lowered the magazine.

“Young man, six reporters asked me those questions before luncheon. Three more asked them after luncheon. One followed me to the station, and another sent his card into my compartment. Do you possess any reason why I should answer you when I refused them?”

Tom considered inventing one. A dramatic plea about the public’s right to know might sound well. A hint that another senator had already spoken might draw a denial. But there was something in August’s level gaze that made tricks seem both foolish and cheap.

“No, sir,” Tom said. “I haven’t.”

“Then we understand each other.”

“Yes, sir. But I should like to remain here, if I may.”

“For what purpose?”

“To give you time to change your mind.”

The senator’s eyebrows rose.

“You are persistent.”

“I need to be.”

“I suppose your editor ordered you not to return without a statement.”

“He ordered me to bring one before five.”

“And if you fail?”

“I have no position to lose.”

This interested the senator.

“No position?”

“Not yet. Mr. Pike said he might give me one if I succeeded.”

“Ah! Then this is an examination.”

“A rather stiff one, sir.”

Senator August leaned back.

“How long have you been a reporter?”

“Since about two o’clock.”

The senator laughed outright.

“And you began by boarding a moving train?”

“I nearly began by missing it.”

“Where is your ticket?”

Tom hesitated.

“That is another difficulty.”

Under questioning, he confessed the state of his finances and his bargain—or attempted bargain—with the conductor. Senator August listened gravely, though amusement remained in his eyes.

“My lad,” he said, “either you have remarkable pluck or remarkably little sense.”

“I hope it is partly pluck.”

“So do I. Sit down.”

Tom took the opposite seat.

“I shall not tell you what occurred at the conference,” the senator continued. “The time for a statement has not arrived. Certain gentlemen must be consulted, and no newspaper is to receive an advantage over another.”

“I understand.”

“Do you?”

“I don’t like it, but I understand it.”

“That is an unusual distinction.”

The senator returned to his magazine. Tom sat quietly.

The train rolled northward through the outskirts of Washington. Rows of brick houses gave way to open ground, and telegraph poles began their measured flight past the window. Somewhere ahead lay Brenton Junction, where Tom would be put off with twenty-seven cents, no news, and a considerable distance between himself and Mr. Pike.

He might make one more appeal. Yet the experienced reporters had appealed, questioned, hinted, and doubtless threatened. His only advantage, if advantage it was, lay in not becoming a nuisance. He watched the fields and tried to think.

The political situation was plain enough. Senator August wished to keep silent until the party leaders had been notified. But silence itself was producing rumors. By evening, the opposition papers might declare that the conference had broken in anger. Markets could react; party men could take sides; tomorrow’s explanations might arrive too late.

If only something forced the senator to speak now!

That was wishing for a miracle, and newspapers could not be run upon miracles. Still, Tom had done all that was possible. He had found his man. He had gained access to him. He was sitting six feet from the secret. Unless—unless fortune favored him, the assignment was hopeless.

The forward door opened, and a trainman entered carrying a yellow envelope.

“Senator August?”

The senator accepted the telegram, tore it open, and read.

His expression changed. The amusement disappeared; two firm lines showed beside his mouth. He read the message again, then glanced at his watch.

“How long before Brenton?” he asked.

“Eight minutes, Senator.”

“Can a telegram be sent from there?”

“Yes, sir. We stop four minutes.”

The trainman went out.

Senator August stared for a moment through the window. Then he turned to Tom.

“You know shorthand?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Have you a notebook?”

Tom had one, together with a pencil worn almost to the metal. He produced them in an instant.

“This message,” said the senator, tapping the telegram, “is from the national chairman. An unauthorized report is circulating in New York that our conference ended in disagreement and that I have resigned from the committee. The report is already affecting two congressional contests. The chairman advises an immediate denial.”

Tom’s fingers tightened around the pencil.

“May I quote you?”

“You may take an official statement. It must be exact.”

“Yes, sir.”

The senator dictated in a measured voice:

“The conference held in Washington this morning by members of the Democratic Congressional Committee reached a complete understanding concerning the currency proposal now before the Senate. Reports of dissension are without foundation. While certain amendments will be recommended, the essential principles of the measure have the support of all persons attending the conference. I have not resigned, nor have I considered resigning, from the committee. A fuller statement will be transmitted tonight to the Associated Press for release tomorrow morning.”

He paused.

“Read that.”

Tom read it aloud. His voice shook on the first sentence and steadied on the second.

“Correct,” said the senator. “Add this: ‘The party enters the approaching campaign united upon the necessity of sound reform and confident of public support.’”

Tom added it.

“Now read the entire statement once more.”

He did so.

Senator August nodded and signed the bottom of the notebook page with a fountain pen.

“You have your news.”

Tom scarcely trusted himself to speak.

“Senator, I—thank you.”

“Thank the national chairman. And perhaps thank that unfortunate habit of yours of boarding trains without tickets.”

The whistle sounded. Houses and sidings appeared outside.

“Brenton,” said the senator. “You had better leave here and telegraph your paper.”

Tom’s delight stumbled over a practical obstacle.

“With twenty-seven cents?”

The senator smiled, drew out a leather pocketbook, and handed him a five-dollar bill.

“I can’t take that, sir.”

“You can repay it when the *Star* pays you.”

“But—”

“The train will not debate the matter. Neither shall I.”

Tom accepted the bill.

“I’ll return every cent tomorrow.”

“I believe you will. One thing more. This statement is yours until eight o’clock tonight. At eight I shall send it to the Associated Press. I cannot properly withhold it longer.”

“That gives us an exclusive.”

“It gives you a bare fighting chance. What you do with it is your affair.”

The brakes ground beneath them. Tom seized his hat and moved toward the door, then turned.

“Senator, when I introduced myself, I said I represented the *Star*. I ought to tell you that Mr. Pike had not hired me.”

“I understood that.”

“Then why did you trust me?”

Senator August folded the telegram.

“Because you told me you had not been hired. A young reporter who is honest when dishonesty might help him is worth trusting with a statement that must be printed accurately. Now go.”

Tom went.

At Brenton Junction he paid the conductor, sent a brief telegram to Mr. Pike—HAVE SIGNED OFFICIAL STATEMENT FROM AUGUST. HOLD SPACE. RETURNING FIRST TRAIN—and discovered that the first train to Washington would not arrive for thirty-five minutes.

Thirty-five minutes!

It was then twenty-eight minutes past three. The local was due in Washington at four-forty-seven, if it kept its schedule. The *Star’s* final regular edition went to press at five.

Tom walked the platform until the stationmaster asked him to stop wearing out the company’s boards. When the local finally appeared, he boarded before it had fully stopped and spent the journey comparing his shorthand notes with the signed statement, though there could be no doubt of the words. He wrote an introduction on copy paper borrowed from the conductor:

“Party unity on the currency question was achieved today at the secret conference of Democratic leaders, according to an exclusive statement made this afternoon to the *Evening Star* by Senator Jonathan August.”

He wrote rapidly, crossed out weak phrases, and wrote again. The train seemed to pause at every farmhouse between Brenton and Washington. At one village it waited while a baggage man rolled three milk cans across the track. Tom regarded those cans with personal hatred.

At last the Capitol dome came into view.

The train entered the station at four-fifty-one—four minutes late. Tom jumped down and ran. This time he had money for a carriage, but none stood immediately at the curb. A streetcar was starting. He caught it, endured two blocks, then sprang off where traffic delayed it and covered the remaining distance on foot.

The office clock said three minutes past five when he burst through the city room gate.

Mr. Pike sat beneath a cloud of pipe smoke. He did not look up.

“You’re late.”

“I have the statement.”

“You’re late,” the editor repeated. “The final plate is on the press.”

Tom’s triumph collapsed. He placed the notebook and his written lead upon the desk.

“It is signed. Senator August says the conference reached complete agreement. They will support the currency bill with amendments. He denies resigning. He won’t give it to the Associated Press until eight tonight.”

Mr. Pike looked up then.

“Until eight?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Who else heard him?”

“No one.”

“Who else has the statement?”

“No one.”

The editor snatched the notebook, read the signed page, and pressed a button.

“Boy!”

The freckled copy boy appeared.

“Take this to the managing editor. Run! Tell him August gives us a three-hour beat and Pike recommends an extra. Then get the copy-cutter.”

The boy vanished.

Mr. Pike seized Tom’s introduction.

“Too many words,” he growled. “The public doesn’t care where you were this afternoon.”

His blue pencil slashed through the sentence.

A man with paste on his sleeves hurried over. Another pulled a telephone toward him and called the composing room. Bells began ringing. Someone shouted, “Hold the front plate!” and from beyond the wall came an answering shout. The newsroom, which had seemed busy before, leaped into a sharper and more magnificent disorder.

Mr. Pike thrust copy paper at Tom.

“Write it. Eight hundred words. First, the result. Second, August’s statement complete. Third, what it means for the bill and the campaign. No autobiography. No adjectives. Make every line earn its type.”

Tom sat at the nearest desk.

His pencil raced. The noise around him ceased to confuse; it drove him forward. Facts arranged themselves in order. The political background he had gathered from weeks of hungry reading now proved useful. He explained the sectional dispute, the danger of a party rupture, and the significance of August’s denial. A copy boy snatched away each sheet as it was finished and carried it to the copy-cutter, who divided it with the enormous shears and sent the slips by pneumatic tube to the composing room.

“Last sheet!” Mr. Pike barked.

Tom wrote the final sentence, read it once, and handed it over.

The editor glanced through it.

“Senator say ‘complete agreement’?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Those exact words?”

“The exact phrase was ‘reached a complete understanding.’”

“Then don’t improve senators. Change it.”

Tom changed it.

Mr. Pike shoved the page at the boy and relit his pipe. For several minutes he said nothing. From below came the gathering thunder of presses beginning a new run.

Tom stood beside the desk, exhausted, dusty, and suddenly conscious that he had eaten nothing since morning.

“Well?” Mr. Pike demanded.

“Sir?”

“Why are you hanging about?”

Tom swallowed.

“I thought—you said if I brought the story—”

“I said I might let you come back tomorrow.”

“Yes, sir.”

Mr. Pike took up his blue pencil and frowned at it as though it had disappointed him.

“Eight o’clock.”

“In the evening?”

“In the morning, Collins. Reporters generally begin before the news is over.”

Tom could only stare.

“Do you mean I’m hired?”

“No,” said Mr. Pike severely. “I mean you are to report here at eight, occupy a desk, take assignments, and draw a salary every Saturday. If you choose to call that being hired, I haven’t time to argue.”

“I’ll be here.”

“You’d better be. And bring back Senator August’s five dollars. The managing editor advanced it when your telegram arrived. We don’t permit our reporters to borrow from their news sources.”

“Our reporters,” Tom repeated.

Mr. Pike’s glare returned.

“Get out and buy yourself a dinner before you faint into the paste pot.”

Tom picked up the five-dollar bill the editor pushed toward him. At the gate, the freckled copy boy met him with the first damp copy of the extra.

Across the top of the page, in black type larger than any words Tom had ever seen connected with his own labor, ran the headline:

**AUGUST DECLARES PARTY UNITED**  
**SECRET CONFERENCE BACKS CURRENCY MEASURE**  
**SPECIAL STATEMENT TO THE EVENING STAR**

Tom stood for a moment holding the warm paper.

Below, the presses roared on, shaking the floor beneath his feet. Newsboys were already crying the extra in the street. The sound came faintly through the windows, rose above the clatter of the city room, and mingled with the steady thunder from below.

At eight o’clock the next morning—indeed, at twenty minutes before eight—Tom Collins reported for work.

The Last Lighthouse Keeper

On the morning the sea climbed the cliffs, Mara Vale found a dead bird in the lighthouse lantern.

It lay beneath the great glass lens, a small gray body with one wing spread, as if it had tried to shield itself from the light. No windows were open. The door to the gallery was locked from within. Yet there it was, salt glittering on its feathers.

Mara picked it up carefully. The bird was cold, but not stiff. Its black eye reflected the revolving beam.

“You’re far from home,” she murmured.

Outside, waves struck the island with the sound of distant cannon fire. Forty meters below, foam leaped across the rocks and blew upward in white ribbons. The island of Saint Orra was scarcely more than a black tooth in the northern sea, crowned by a lighthouse, a keeper’s cottage, and a graveyard in which seven keepers slept beneath stones polished smooth by rain.

Mara carried the bird down the iron staircase.

The lighthouse had been built in 1848 and automated in 1996, but storms had a way of making automation seem like an optimistic theory. For the past eleven years, Mara had lived alone on Saint Orra as caretaker, electrician, weather observer, and unofficial keeper of promises no one remembered making.

Every six weeks, a supply boat arrived from the mainland. Twice a year, inspectors came to test the emergency systems. They usually stayed less than an hour.

A brass telephone hung in the kitchen, linked to the mainland by an undersea cable. That morning it rang before Mara had finished boiling water.

She lifted the receiver.

“Saint Orra Light.”

At first there was only static. Then a man’s voice emerged, faint and breathless.

“Miss Vale? This is Daniel Harker, Maritime Authority.”

“I know who you are, Mr. Harker.”

“Yes. Of course.” Papers rustled. “There’s a severe system moving east. Worse than forecast. The supply vessel has been recalled.”

“I assumed it would be.”

“We want you to shut down nonessential equipment and prepare for evacuation.”

Mara looked through the kitchen window. The horizon had disappeared. Sea and sky had become a single mass of iron.

“What evacuation?”

A pause.

“Helicopter, if conditions allow.”

“They won’t.”

“Then remain in the cottage. The lighthouse structure may be unsafe.”

“The lighthouse has survived every storm for a hundred and seventy-eight years.”

“This is not every storm.”

Mara wrapped the telephone cord around one finger. On the table, the dead bird seemed to be listening.

Harker continued. “There’s something else. You should know before the cable fails. The Authority approved decommissioning last night.”

Mara said nothing.

“Saint Orra will be dark by the end of the month,” he said. “The new satellite beacons make it redundant.”

“Redundant.”

“I’m sorry.”

“You always say that before something permanent.”

“Mara—”

The line cracked violently.

“Miss Vale, please confirm you understand the evacuation order.”

“I understand it.”

The connection died.

Mara kept the receiver to her ear until the silence became foolish. Then she returned it to its cradle.

For eleven years she had known the lighthouse would close. Everyone had. Ships carried digital charts, satellite navigation, collision alarms, and instruments that could locate a vessel within meters in the middle of an ocean. The old beam, visible for twenty-four nautical miles in clear weather, had become ceremonial.

Yet sailors still looked for it.

Mara knew because some of them sent letters.

Saw your light through the snow last December.

We’d lost power north of the shoals. That flash told us where we were.

My father used to say Saint Orra blinked like God keeping one eye open.

She kept the letters in a biscuit tin beneath her bed.

The storm arrived in earnest by noon.

Rain struck sideways. The cottage walls trembled, and the wind screamed in the chimney with such force that soot fell onto the hearth. Mara secured the shutters, checked the generator, and filled every container with fresh water.

Then she buried the bird beside the path.

The ground was thin there, little more than peat between slabs of rock. She dug with a hand trowel, laid the body in the hole, and covered it while the storm tugged at her coat.

As she stood, she noticed something caught in the heather.

It was a strip of red cloth.

Mara pulled it free. The fabric had been torn from a larger garment, and along one edge ran a line of tiny brass buttons. It was soaked, but not faded.

A memory opened inside her.

A red coat on a station platform. Her younger brother Elias, fifteen years old, waving with both arms as the train carried her away. He had always waved too long, continuing after everyone else had stopped, as though departures could be undone through persistence.

Three months later, he drowned.

His fishing boat was found drifting south of Saint Orra with no one aboard. The sea returned one boot, a broken oar, and a square of red sailcloth.

Mara stared at the cloth in her hand.

It could not be the same piece. That had happened twenty-two years ago, and Elias’s boat had gone down eighty miles away. Storms collected strange debris: flags, ropes, cargo labels, messages in bottles. Once, after a winter gale, Mara had found a wooden door on the eastern shore, freshly painted blue, with the key still in its lock.

She folded the red cloth and put it in her pocket.

At two in the afternoon, the main generator failed.

The lights in the cottage flickered out. The refrigerator fell silent. Somewhere above, the rotating mechanism slowed, and the lighthouse beam stopped over the western sea.

Mara put on her boots and climbed to the engine room.

Diesel fumes burned her throat. The control panel showed no fuel pressure. She checked the line and found the intake clogged with black sediment. It took forty minutes to clear, working by the light of a battery lantern while the walls shook around her.

When she restarted the engine, it coughed twice and caught.

Power returned. Above her, the mechanism began to turn.

Mara went outside to confirm the beam. The wind nearly threw her against the tower. She gripped the railing and looked up.

Light swept over her, brilliant and brief.

One, two, three, darkness.

One, two, three, darkness.

Saint Orra’s pattern.

She was turning back when she saw a person standing by the graveyard wall.

The figure was small and thin, wearing a red coat.

Mara froze.

Rain streamed across her face. The figure stood less than thirty meters away, but the storm obscured its features. It lifted one hand.

Not waving.

Pointing.

Out to sea.

Mara followed the gesture. Between walls of rain, she glimpsed a light low on the water. It flashed twice, vanished, then flashed twice again.

A distress signal.

When she looked back, the figure was gone.

Mara ran to the cottage and seized the telephone.

No signal.

She tried the radio. Emergency channel sixteen hissed with static. She adjusted the frequency, called the coastguard, and received nothing.

The light at sea appeared again.

Two flashes.

Darkness.

Two flashes.

She took binoculars from the shelf, though visibility was almost useless. From the lighthouse gallery, she scanned the western shoals.

At first she saw only white water. Then the beam revolved, and for one second it illuminated a vessel caught between waves.

A small cargo ship.

Its bow was low, its deck tilted, and smoke streamed from the stern. It was drifting toward the Bellman Reefs, where the cliffs continued invisibly beneath the sea in rows of black stone.

Mara searched the charts. At its present course, the vessel would strike the outer reef within an hour.

She tried the radio again.

“Unidentified vessel west of Saint Orra, this is Saint Orra Light. Respond.”

Static.

“Vessel west of Saint Orra, alter course south-southwest. You are approaching Bellman Reefs.”

Nothing.

A burst of sound came through, too broken to understand.

Mara leaned close.

“Repeat.”

“…engine… steering gone…”

“State number of persons aboard.”

“…seven…”

Then the signal vanished.

Seven people.

Mara knew the reef. At low tide, its tallest rocks emerged like the backs of animals. At high tide, the entire field disappeared beneath turbulent water. No lifeboat could cross it in this weather, and no helicopter could hover in such wind.

The cargo ship could not steer.

The lighthouse could warn it, but not save it.

Unless—

Mara opened a cabinet beneath the chart table and removed a roll of old plans. The paper was yellow at the edges and smelled of dust. She spread one sheet under the lamp.

Before automation, Saint Orra had possessed a foghorn mounted on the western platform. Three compressed-air blasts every ninety seconds. The horn had been deactivated years ago, but the pipes remained. So did the manual valve in the lower service tunnel.

Sound traveled strangely through storms. If she altered the sequence, she might guide the ship along the narrow channel between the outer and inner reefs.

It was a desperate idea. The channel was barely wide enough for a vessel of that size, and the ship would need enough engine power to control its drift.

But desperation was simply hope with its sleeves rolled up.

Mara descended to the service tunnel.

Water already covered the floor. The lighthouse foundation had been built directly into the rock, and narrow passages ran below the tower to storage chambers and drainage shafts. At the far western end, behind a rusted door, stood the foghorn compressor.

Mara had inspected it once, ten years earlier. It looked less like a machine than the skeleton of one.

She opened the fuel line, checked the oil, and connected a portable starter battery. Nothing happened.

She struck the housing with a wrench.

“Don’t be theatrical.”

She tried again.

The motor turned with a low groan. Rust flakes fell from the pipes. Then the compressor shuddered into life, filling the chamber with a pounding roar.

Mara laughed aloud.

She climbed back to the radio.

“Vessel west of Saint Orra, can you hear me?”

A weak voice answered. “…hear you.”

“I can guide you through the reef by horn. Do you have any power?”

“Emergency engine. Three knots, maybe four. No instruments.”

“Can you see the lighthouse?”

“When waves allow.”

“Turn until the light is directly off your port side. Keep it there. Listen for the horn. One blast means turn starboard. Two means port. A long blast means hold course. Do you understand?”

Static swallowed the reply.

“Do you understand?”

“Yes.”

“What is your vessel’s name?”

“Mercy Bell.”

Mara closed her eyes briefly.

Of course it was.

She had learned long ago that the sea had a sense of humor, though not a kind one.

She returned to the horn chamber. From there she could not see the ship, so she carried an extension cable and the old camera monitor used during maintenance. The image flickered, showing the western sea from the gallery.

The Mercy Bell drifted in and out of view.

Mara opened the valve.

The foghorn spoke.

Its voice was enormous. It passed through stone and bone, a deep cry that seemed to rise from the island itself.

One long blast.

Hold course.

The ship moved slowly toward the outer reef. Mara watched the screen, comparing its position with landmarks she knew better than the lines of her own hands: Widow’s Tooth, the Broken Crown, the flat slab called the Table.

A wave turned the vessel north.

One blast. Starboard.

Nothing happened.

She sounded again.

The ship corrected just before its bow reached a line of breaking water.

“Come on,” Mara whispered. “Come on.”

For twenty minutes, she guided it by sound.

Two blasts. Port.

Long blast. Hold.

One blast. Starboard.

Every signal was an act of faith. She could not know whether the crew heard her correctly or whether the next wave would undo everything. The monitor blinked off twice. Each time, Mara struck the cable connection and prayed to no one in particular.

The Mercy Bell entered the channel.

Now black rocks rose on both sides. Waves crashed over the deck. A container tore loose and slid into the sea.

The ship turned too far east.

Mara sounded two blasts.

No correction.

Two blasts again.

The bow continued toward the inner reef.

She ran upstairs to the radio.

“Mercy Bell, turn port!”

“…cannot… engine…”

The words dissolved.

“Turn port now!”

“…propeller fouled…”

The ship was less than five minutes from the rocks.

Mara looked at the lighthouse controls.

The beam continued its measured rotation, indifferent as a clock. One, two, three, darkness.

The ship needed something stronger than a warning. It needed a direction.

Beside the main controls was the manual brake used to stop the lens during maintenance. Mara pulled it. The great lens slowed and halted, facing north.

She released the brake, let the beam turn halfway, then stopped it again—this time pointing directly at the southern opening of the channel.

A road of light appeared across the water.

She spoke into the radio.

“Mercy Bell, follow the beam.”

“We can’t turn.”

“Use the sea anchor. Drop it off your port bow.”

A long silence.

Then: “Anchor line may not hold.”

“It doesn’t have to hold. It has to turn you.”

Through the monitor, Mara saw figures moving on deck. They were tiny shadows in orange survival suits. A line uncoiled. Something heavy vanished over the port side.

For a moment, nothing changed.

Then the bow began to swing.

The ship turned toward the beam.

A wave struck its starboard side and pushed it forward into the channel. The anchor line snapped, but it had done its work.

The Mercy Bell passed between the rocks with no more than fifteen meters to spare.

Mara sounded the horn continuously.

Not a signal now, but a celebration.

The ship emerged south of the reef into deeper water.

Mara grabbed the radio.

“You’re clear. Keep south-southwest. The coastguard station is forty miles. They’ll find you when the storm breaks.”

No answer came at first.

Then a different voice, a woman’s, said, “Saint Orra, we see your light.”

Mara held the radio with both hands.

“Good.”

“We thought the lighthouse was unmanned.”

“It isn’t yet.”

The signal faded.

Mara remained beside the controls, holding the beam south-southwest until the vessel disappeared beyond the rain.

Only then did she notice the water around her boots.

The service tunnel had flooded. Seawater poured up the stairwell and across the engine-room floor. Somewhere below, the compressor coughed and died. The main generator followed seconds later.

Darkness filled the tower.

Mara switched on her battery lantern.

The tide had risen higher than any recorded level. Waves were entering through the western drainage shafts. If the fuel tanks flooded, the emergency systems would fail. If the foundation doors gave way, the pressure might crack the lower tower.

She climbed to the cottage for the satellite beacon kept for evacuation.

The cottage door stood open.

She was certain she had locked it.

Inside, rain had blown across the floor. The biscuit tin lay beneath the table, its lid open. Letters were scattered like fallen birds.

A boy stood by the cold fireplace.

He was fifteen years old. His dark hair dripped seawater. He wore the red coat from the station platform, though Mara now remembered that Elias had never owned such a coat. Memory and invention had stitched one around him.

“You stayed too long,” he said.

Mara could not breathe.

Elias smiled. One front tooth overlapped the other. She had forgotten that.

“You aren’t here,” she managed.

“No.”

“Did you bring the bird?”

“No.”

“The cloth?”

“No.”

“Then why are you here?”

He shrugged in the careless way he had as a boy. “You needed someone to tell you.”

“Tell me what?”

“To leave.”

Lightning whitened the cottage. For an instant, Mara saw only the empty room.

Then he was there again.

“You always think staying is the brave thing,” he said.

“I left you.”

“You went to college.”

“I should have come home.”

“You couldn’t have stopped the sea.”

“I might have been with you.”

“And then Mam would have lost us both.”

The lighthouse shuddered. A deep cracking sound came from below.

Elias glanced toward the door.

“Mara.”

She wanted to move to him, but fear held her still—not fear of the storm, but fear that he would vanish if she crossed the room.

“I kept the light,” she said.

“I know.”

“For you.”

“I know that too.”

“Was it enough?”

He looked older then. Not in his face, but in his eyes.

“It was a light,” he said. “It wasn’t a life.”

Another crack shook the island. Plaster fell from the ceiling.

Mara reached for him.

Her hand passed through cold air.

The room was empty.

She stood alone among the letters.

Then she moved.

She stuffed emergency supplies into a waterproof bag, fastened her survival suit, and activated the satellite beacon. The display blinked red: signal transmitted.

Outside, the eastern cliff offered the only shelter from the wind. Mara crawled toward the stone equipment shed where an inflatable life raft was stored. Rain hammered her back. Behind her, the lighthouse beam remained dark.

She dragged the raft to the sheltered slope and pulled the inflation cord. The yellow canopy burst open.

A sound like thunder came from beneath the island.

The lighthouse tilted.

Not far—perhaps only a few centimeters—but Mara saw it clearly against the sky. A vertical line that had defined her world for eleven years leaned toward the sea.

She climbed into the raft and cut the tether.

Water had covered the eastern rocks, transforming the island into a chain of low, black shapes. The raft lifted, spun, and was carried away.

Mara looked back.

The storm drew a gray curtain around Saint Orra. The cottage vanished first. Then the graveyard wall. The lighthouse remained, dark and leaning, its glass lantern catching stray flashes of lightning.

For one impossible second, a light appeared at the top.

Not the electric beam. A smaller light, warm and gold, like a lamp carried by hand.

Beside it stood the silhouette of a boy, waving with both arms.

Mara waved back.

She continued even after the island disappeared.

At dawn, a coastguard helicopter found her nine miles south of Saint Orra.

The storm had passed, leaving the sea strangely smooth. From the air, Mara saw wreckage scattered across the water: timber, barrels, the blue roof of the equipment shed. Of the lighthouse, only the upper gallery remained above the tide.

The Mercy Bell reached port under tow that afternoon. All seven crew members survived.

Weeks later, Maritime Authority officials held an inquiry in a white room overlooking the harbor. They asked Mara why she had ignored the evacuation order, why she had activated obsolete machinery, why she had manually interfered with the automated lens.

Mara answered every question.

At the end, Daniel Harker switched off the recorder.

“There’s one thing I don’t understand,” he said. “The foghorn compressor was inspected after the collapse.”

“What was left of it.”

“Yes. The fuel line had been disconnected for at least twenty years. The tank was empty.”

Mara looked through the window. On the harbor wall, gulls leaned into the wind.

“Then your inspectors made a mistake.”

“Three separate engineers reached the same conclusion.”

“Engineers enjoy agreeing with one another.”

Harker studied her. “The crew heard the horn.”

“I know.”

“So did people on the mainland. Forty miles away.”

“It was a loud horn.”

He waited, but Mara offered nothing more.

The Authority replaced Saint Orra with a floating satellite beacon: a steel pillar with a red light and no room inside for memory. Charts were updated. Reports were filed. The old lighthouse became a black outline beneath the sea.

Mara did not return to the island.

She moved to a village on the northern coast and rented a house with a green door. For the first time in years, she had neighbors. Children knocked to ask if they could retrieve balls from her garden. Someone invited her to dinner every Friday. She bought a blue bicycle and learned to sleep without the sound of waves striking rock beneath her bed.

The biscuit tin survived the storm inside her waterproof bag.

She kept it on a shelf, but she no longer opened it every night.

One winter evening, almost a year after the lighthouse fell, a parcel arrived without a return address. Inside was a strip of red cloth edged with tiny brass buttons and a note from the captain of the Mercy Bell.

Found this tangled in our anchor chain after the storm. Thought it might belong to Saint Orra.

Mara carried the cloth to the beach.

The sun was setting. Far offshore, the new beacon began to flash its simple red warning.

She stood at the edge of the water, remembering a boy on a station platform, waving long after the train had begun to move.

For years, she had mistaken that memory for a command to return.

Now she understood it differently.

He had not been calling her back.

He had been saying goodbye.

Mara placed the red cloth on the water. A wave lifted it, folded it once, and carried it out beneath the darkening sky.

She watched until she could no longer see it.

Then, before night fully arrived, she turned toward the lights of the village and went home.
